Nevertheless, the substantial background fluorescence serves as an indication of polymer degradation and the formation of highly absorptive moieties.156 To better distinguish the source of degradation, additional TCC samples were subjected to isolated instances of high-intensity ultra-violet (UV) irradiation (50W, 356nm R.H. <10%) or damp heat in dark (30°C, 90-100% R.H.) for 500 hours. As shown in Figure 21a, high-intensity UV exposure results in a significant increase in the background fluorescence, with the accompanying broadband (1,850 cm-1 to 2,150 cm-1) after background removal and normalization (Figure 21b). In contrast, the Raman spectrum of the damp-heat aged sample shows negligible fluorescence and a near-identical spectrum after normalization (Figure 21c and d). These observations indicate that the epoxy degradation process is primarily driven by photo-oxidation,153 corroborated by the unchanged Raman spectra for the shaded region (located under the sample holder mounting frame) within the outdoor exposed TCC sample (Figure 20a). The selection of a more durable polymer that does not contain aromatic moieties (e.g., Masterbond epoxy), better stabilization chemistry, or the use of UV filters should reduce photooxidative aging.
